fields.Q1:
WHAT IS STANDING AROUND THIS ROOM MADE OF?**
Large cut stone blocks, roughly 32 art px square, dry-laid with hairline joints. Smooth-faced — you'd put a hand on flat, cool, slightly dusty stone with nothing on it.
fields.Q1_WHY:
At 6× on the lit band `x 440–700, y 384–432` the blocks are near-flat colour with a soft vertical value drift and *no* grain, aggregate, pitting, chisel mark or noise of any kind. Course lines run at `y≈392` and block-to-block seams are 1–3 art px of slightly darker tone (measured: `x 565–571, y 390–421` is a 3-art-px dark gap, hard-edged, unshaded inside). Every block carries one identical 1-px stepped diagonal tick in its upper-left corner. So: cut stone, but the face itself is unarticulated.

---
fields.Q2:
SOLID MASS, OR FLAT PATTERN AROUND THE EDGE?**
**Flat pattern.** Not ambiguous — measured.

At `x=370→391, y=340`: wall top reads 101–109, then a **single art-pixel** seam at `x 375–376` (lum 31), then corridor floor at 41–87. One pixel is the entire boundary. The east side is the same (`x 437`, lum 101 between 133 and 131).

The horizontal wall at `x=200` reads: void 7 → wall top 37–60 (`y 390–421`) → **2 art px** of flat black rule (`y 422–425`, lum 12) → floor 23–30. That black rule is the only thickness cue in the frame, it is dead straight and uniform across all 750 px, and it has no gradient — it's a ruler line, not a face and not a shadow.

Value confirms it. At `y=370`, wall mean ≈ 110, corridor floor mean ≈ 97. The walls are **brighter than the floor beside them** at the same distance from the lamp. Nothing occludes, nothing sits above anything.

---
fields.Q3:
WHERE EXACTLY DOES THE GROUND STOP?**
Two transitions, both minimal.

*North edge of the room*, at `x=200`: floor holds ~23–30 down to `y=426`; `y 422–425` is the black rule (lum 12–13); `y 390–421` is wall top (37–60); `y≤389` is void (7). **Four screen pixels / two art pixels** carry the entire floor→wall event. What changes across it: value drops 30→12, rises 12→60. No hue shift, no bevel, no ambient occlusion ramp, no lip.

*Corridor walls*, `x=375–376` and `x=437–438`: **two screen pixels / one art pixel**, value dip only. Block scale changes from ~16 art px (floor, with mortar grid) to ~32 art px (wall) across that one pixel — which is doing more work than the value is.

---
fields.Q4:
WHAT IS HOLDING THIS PLACE TOGETHER?**
**NOTHING.**

I scanned every lit surface at 6× — the E–W band `y 384–432` full width, both corridor columns `y 140–388`, and the ambient-lit band `y 60–140` brightened 7×. There is no rope, no lashing, no driven pin, no plate, no hide, no timber, no bracing, no wedge, no strap. Not one. The vertical dark bar at `x 565–571` that I checked as a candidate pin is a block seam. The only non-stone elements in the frame are nine copies of one black parallelogram stamp, and those read as holes, not as hardware.

For a level held by a company that has been repairing this line for four hundred years with rope and pins, that is the loudest thing in the picture. **100% of the wall vocabulary is damage; 0% is intervention.**

---
fields.Q5:
BUILT, OR REPEATED?**
**Repeated.** Same lattice, same stamps, same rate.

Nine instances of one black parallelogram sprite — identical silhouette, identical 1-px light streak on the upper-left edge, identical stipple scatter below-right, same orientation, never mirrored or rotated — at screen `(24,92) (0,14) (316,142) (660,78) (188,398) (720,106) (444,232) (440,396) (692,524)`. I placed them side by side; they are the same object.

The corner chamfer tick appears in the upper-left of every block, same length, same corner.

And the damage rate is flat. Crack coverage measured per region: E–W wall band **7.4%**, west corridor column **9.6%**, east corridor column **6.2%**, top band **7.9%**. Four separate structures, one number. Cracks don't concentrate at corners, don't follow spans, don't cluster at the corridor mouth where a wall would actually be stressed. They are a texture rate, not a history.

The cracks aren't literal copy-paste (best non-self template match ≈ 70%), so they're generated from one recipe — but one recipe with one behaviour: a 1-px black line wandering top-to-bottom, never horizontal, never branching, never terminating at a joint.

---
fields.Q6:
WOULD YOU BELIEVE THIS SHIPPED?**
**YES.**

Merely competent. The palette is disciplined, the light falloff is clean, the block rhythm doesn't tile visibly. But the thing that would make it genuinely good — a wall that reads as mass from across the room — is absent, and the fiction's single most distinctive element (four centuries of ugly, expert, improvised repair) has not been drawn at all.

---
fields.Q7:
WHAT CAN YOU ACTUALLY SEE ON THE STANDING SURFACES AT 1:1?**

*Legible at 1:1:*
- The black crack squiggles. High contrast, unmistakable, everywhere.
- The 2-art-px black rule under the E–W wall — the strongest single line in the frame.
- Block seams, marginally, in the brightest zone only.
- The parallelogram stamps at `(444,232)` and `(188,398)` — visible as dark smudges; I could not tell what they were.

*Only on magnification:*
- The corner chamfer ticks — invisible at 1:1, all of them.
- The 1-px course line at `y≈392`.
- The soft vertical gradient inside each block (at 1:1 it reads as unspecific blotchiness, not as stone).
- That the parallelogram is a repeated sprite with a light streak and a stipple tail.

**The block face itself is blank at 1:1.** Strip out the cracks and there is nothing on the stone. That is the honest answer.

Distance changes only whether you see it at all, not what you see. In the ambient band `y 60–140` (lum 9–13) nothing is legible without a 7× brightness lift; brightened, it's the same two elements. There is no near/far detail hierarchy — the same crack sprite at the same weight is used at lum 130 and at lum 12.
fields.Q8:
ANYTHING YOUR EYE KEEPS RETURNING TO?**
Four things, in order of how hard they pull:

1. **The vertical crack squiggle.** ~34,400 pixels of it, 4.9% of the whole frame. On every block, at a constant rate. Dense examples: `(258,404)`, `(140,404)`, `(618,396)`, `(460,340)`, and the whole band `y 70–132` where I counted ~30 separate squiggles across 750 px.
2. **The black parallelogram**, nine times, listed in Q5. Once you see the light streak on its top-left corner you cannot stop seeing it.
3. **The chamfer tick, upper-left of every block.** Same corner, every time.
4. **The black rule at `y 422–425`.** Perfectly straight, perfectly uniform, edge to edge. It's the only thing telling me a wall has a bottom, and it's a drawn line.

---
fields.Q9:
WHAT IS BEYOND THE WALLS?**
**Two different beyonds, and neither is stone.**

*Nothing.* `x 0–310, y 134–389` and `x 503–750, y 134–389` are luminance **1–3** — effectively pure black, with hard axis-aligned rectangular edges. At `y=250` the step is `x=310` lum 3 → `x=311` lum 26, one pixel, no transition at all. That is not dark rock and it is not light falloff — it is a hole cut in the image.

*More of the same.* `y 0–133`, full width, sits at a flat ambient 9–13 and, brightened, is exactly the same big-block cracked wall material, plus a corridor. Same stone, same crack recipe.

So the answer the picture gives is: **beyond the wall is either the identical material, or an absence with a straight edge.** It never once suggests mass, depth, or rock you couldn't walk through. Worse — the black regions are *darker* than the walls, so on first read the walls look like a lit walkway and the void looks like the drop.

The boundary between those two states is a tile-granular visibility mask that cuts straight across at `y=134` from `x=0` to `x=310`, slicing through the middle of blocks and ignoring the structure entirely.

---
fields.Q10:
COULD YOU TELL A WAY THROUGH WITHOUT WALKING INTO IT?**
Found it: `x 377–440`, running north from `y≈388` to `y≈60`, about one tile wide against a 750 px screen. It opens onto an east–west run at the top of the frame.

**I read it as a passage — but weakly, and not for the right reasons.** What made the difference was the **change in block scale** (fine ~16-px grid with mortar inside the gap, large ~32-px flat blocks either side) and the fact that the gap is centred in the frame. That's it.

What did *not* help: lighting. At `y=340` the corridor floor reads 41–87 while the wall tops beside it read 101–109 — the passage is *darker than its own walls*. At `y=180`, `y=240` and `y=350` corridor and wall are within noise of each other. The lamp travels up the wall exactly as far as it travels up the corridor. If I had to call a passage from value alone I would have called it wrong.

Between "passage" and "notch in a pattern" I'd put myself at maybe 70/30 at 1:1. On a phone, in motion, that is not enough — and this is the case the question is actually about: telling a way through from a dead end before committing a turn to it.

---
fields.Q11:
HAS ANYTHING HAPPENED TO THIS STRUCTURE?**
It has been cracked, uniformly, by nothing in particular, and then left exactly as it was.

What I read it from: crack coverage is 6.2–9.6% on all four separate wall regions — one rate, applied flat. Every crack runs top-to-bottom regardless of the block it's on, crosses joints as though the joints weren't there, and — the decisive one — **crosses the wall's own base.** At `x≈267` a single crack starts at `y=390` on the wall top, runs down through the black rule at `y=422` without a break, an offset, or a change of weight, and continues onto the floor to `y=452`. Same line, both sides. A crack cannot do that unless the wall and the floor are the same flat surface.

There is one pale lumpy shape at `(283–297, 422–432)` sitting on the base line that might be spall. Nothing else has fallen, nothing has shifted, nothing has been shored, nothing has been patched, nothing has been walked smooth in one place and not another. There is damage but there is no *event* — no history, no direction, no one having been here.

For a place in continuous heavy use since before records, held under repair by soldiers for four hundred years, the structure shows neither the use nor the repair.

---
fields.CULL: Walls and floor render on one flat plane at equal value — a crack crosses the wall base uninterrupted.
fields.FLIP LIST:
- Render a real inner face on every wall: 4–6 art px of darker, separately-lit block edge below each wall run, plus a cast shadow on the floor that falls off with the lamp. Replace the flat 2-art-px black rule at `y 422–425`.
- Terminate every crack at the wall/floor boundary and at block joints. Kill the run at `x≈267` that goes from `y=390` straight through to `y=452`.
- Drop wall-top luminance to ~55–65% of floor at equal light distance, and make the corridor floor at `x 377–440` read brighter than the columns flanking it. Currently `y=370`: walls ≈110, floor ≈97 — inverted.
- Put the orcs' work on the walls: driven pins, lashed rope, salvaged timber shoring at the corridor mouth `(375–440, 388)` and along the E–W run. At least one repair per screen, clearly not stone.
- Vary or retire the two repeated stamps — the nine identical black parallelograms and the upper-left chamfer tick on every block — and break the flat 6–10% crack rate so damage clusters at corners, openings and spans instead of spreading evenly.

*Model: Claude Opus 5 (1M context).*
